body.text: Australians to gain right to sue social media giants under Labor-Greens deal
In short:
Labor has secured support for laws requiring social media companies to do more to protect Australians online.
The deal gives people the right to take tech giants to court over harm they suffer.
What's next?
The digital duty of care legislation is due to pass the Senate with the Greens' support.
Australians will be able to directly sue social media giants for harm under changes to the federal government's proposed new digital safety laws.

Labor reached a deal with the Greens today to pass its digital duty of care legislation through the Senate, after agreeing to a series of amendments to increase penalties and give people greater power to hold tech giants to account.
The government agreed to give Australians a "private right of action" that would allow them to sue social media companies for harm suffered online.

Australia's current online safety laws largely rely on the eSafety commissioner to hold tech companies to account, leaving individuals seeking compensation to navigate complex and largely untested avenues under existing negligence and consumer protection laws.
In the United States, where courts have greater scope to award damages designed to punish companies as well as compensate victims, thousands of lawsuits have been brought against social media giants.
In one landmark case this year, a jury awarded $US6 million (almost $9 million) to a young woman who suffered harm from social media addiction.

Communications Minister Anika Wells said she imagined it would be "fairly rare" that Australians sued big tech, while the Greens declared they would see the companies "in court" if they failed to lift safety standards.
Social media companies to face higher fines

Under Labor's deal with the Greens, the maximum penalty for breaching the duty would be raised to up to 5 per cent of a platform's global revenue, rather than Labor's initial proposal of up to $109.2 million.
The amendments also grant the government rule-making powers to establish a digital complaints ombudsman in the future to handle small claims and resolve minor issues.
Other changes agreed to include requiring platforms to consider "addictive" design features, such as endless doomscrolling, in the risk assessments they provide to the eSafety Commission.
Ms Wells said she hoped the digital duty of care would fuel a "cultural change" in how social media tech companies were accountable for the harms caused by their products.
"My message to parents is: we understand you. We have your backs," she said.
"This is about that phone that is under the pillow at night when you can't get to it.
"This is about kids being radicalised on a school bus on their way home.
"This is about a child sitting across from you on the couch and you not being able to see what is on that screen.
"We built this digital duty of care for you."

Labor's proposed duty would require online platforms such as Facebook, TikTok and Instagram to take reasonable steps to prevent a range of harms to children, including bullying, misogyny and content promoting eating disorders.
Big tech would also have to limit adults' exposure to serious harms such as threats of violence, stalking and the non-consensual sharing of intimate images.
The bill would also let Australians aged 16 and over switch off algorithm-driven feeds and see only content from accounts they chose to follow.

Asked if she was anticipating blowback from the Trump administration, which has taken issue with attempts to regulate US-based tech companies, Ms Wells revealed she had briefed US Ambassador to Australia David Brat about the latest changes.
"It has been a long signalled intent of our government that we would pass these [laws] because online safety is such a priority for us," she said.
Greens say duty changes take power 'back' from big tech
Greens communications spokeswoman Sarah Hanson-Young said social media giants could pay billions of dollars for the harm they caused.
"Like every other company selling products in Australia, big tech will finally be held responsible for the harm that their products cause," she said.
Senator Hanson-Young said if big tech did not "clean up their act" there "must be class actions" brought against them.
"Big tech has a choice now, work to make your platform safer, work with parents to be able to make the engagement online with their kids safer," she said.
"Or we'll see you in court."
Greens leader David Shoebridge said the amendments secured by his party were "taking power back" from largely US-based corporations on behalf of Australians.

"This is a powerful demonstration of how you get results in politics, as Greens we have campaigned for a duty of care for years and now we will help deliver laws with real teeth that put people ahead of big tech profits," he said.
On Monday, Labor also flagged small businesses with low-risk websites would be exempted from requirements under the duty.
The Coalition has remained opposed to the bill, raising concerns about freedom of speech.
